anchor: GS2.5 Governance: transparency, accountability, e-governance; GS3.5 Environment: pollution and waste
argumentsAgainst: A cleanliness campaign can become a one-time compliance exercise if targets are not followed by routine maintenance, audited disposal chains and measurable post-campaign outcomes.
Scrap monetisation alone does not establish safe e-waste management; environmental compliance and traceability remain necessary.
File weeding must preserve legally required records and avoid weakening institutional memory or accountability.
argumentsFor: The campaign links cleanliness with administrative efficiency, space optimisation, digitisation and waste-to-wealth outcomes.
Competitive targets and reporting can improve accountability within public-sector organisations.
Scientific segregation and disposal of e-waste can reduce unsafe handling while recovering usable material.
Removing redundant material and reviewing records can release office space and streamline procedures.
background: Special Campaign 6 is a time-bound cleanliness and administrative reform exercise covering government offices and public-sector entities. Ministry of Coal materials describe its implementation phase as running from 2 October to 31 October 2

indiaImplications: Public-sector entities can convert dormant material and underused office space into administrative and fiscal value, subject to transparent disposal procedures.
Scientific e-waste handling can support pollution reduction and resource recovery, while poor segregation can shift environmental risks to informal or unsafe processing.
Digitised and better-managed records may improve retrieval, responsiveness and institutional continuity, but disposal protocols must protect retention obligations.
The approach offers a replicable governance model for ministries, CPSEs and subordinate offices, with outcomes assessed through independent verification rather than headline numbers alone.

example.text: If a public office identifies obsolete equipment, segregates e-waste, sends it through an authorised disposal channel, digitises eligible records and reuses the released space, one coordinated exercise can produce environmental and administrative benefits. This is a hypothetical illustration, not a reported event.

pocketRead.excerpt: The Ministry of Coal’s Special Campaign 6 connects cleanliness, scrap disposal, e-waste management and administrative record-keeping with measurable public-sector outcomes.

question.answer: It can improve governance by making waste, space and records administratively visible and measurable; safeguards are needed to ensure authorised e-waste disposal, lawful record retention, transparent auctions and continuing maintenance.
question.prompt: How can a public-sector cleanliness campaign become an instrument of accountable governance rather than a symbolic exercise?

sections.heading: From housekeeping to resource governance
paragraphs: On 26 October 2026, the Ministry of Coal reported that its CPSEs had achieved milestones under Special Campaign 6, including cleaning 130.16 lakh square feet and generating approximately ₹53.94 crore from scrap disposal. The reported outputs show how a cleanliness drive can connect workplace management with resource recovery.

The campaign’s practical mechanism is to identify and clear scrap, handle e-waste, review records and improve space utilisation. Its limitation is that reported outputs do not by themselves establish the durability of maintenance or the environmental quality of every disposal pathway.

sections.heading: Administrative value and safeguards
paragraphs: For UPSC analysis, the campaign illustrates outcome-oriented governance: targets can make departmental housekeeping measurable, while digitisation and file review can reduce procedural friction. Scrap disposal may also return value to the exchequer.

The same model requires safeguards. E-waste needs scientific and authorised processing; record weeding must follow retention rules; and disposal figures should be auditable. The broader lesson is to institutionalise monitoring after the campaign period ends.

staticDefinition: Special Campaign 6 is a time-bound public-administration exercise that operationalises cleanliness through identification and disposal of waste, management of e-waste and scrap, optimisation of office space, and review or digitisation of records.[1][5]

advisory_notes: The note’s reported figures and title are supported by the supplied PIB extract [P1].
The 2–31 October 2026 implementation period is supported by DPE’s official release [3], but it is not present in the supplied Coal extract.
The proposed GS2.5 and GS3.5 tags are defensible syllabus mappings; GS4.6 is relevant but indirect and should be treated as an ethical-governance linkage.
“Digitisation” is broader than the Coal extract, which reports review of physical and e-files; retain it as analysis rather than a reported outcome.
“Revenue to the exchequer” is stated in [P1], while “fiscal value” and “scrap monetisation” are reasonable analytical interpretations, not independently demonstrated outcomes.
The claims about authorised recyclers, chain of custody, retention schedules, auctions, dashboards and grievance channels are recommendations, not facts established by the release.

The pocketRead headline and deck accurately summarise the reported linkage, but “waste recovery” may overstate the evidence because the release reports scrap disposal, not recovery or recycling rates.
The hypothetical example is clearly labelled as an illustration and should remain separate from the Coal CPSEs’ reported actions.

wayForward: Define output, outcome and maintenance indicators separately, including safe e-waste processing and post-campaign upkeep.
Use authorised recyclers, documented chain-of-custody procedures and transparent disposal or auction mechanisms.
Apply record-retention schedules before weeding files and preserve essential institutional data through secure digitisation.
Publish periodic dashboards with independent verification and grievance or audit channels.
